title: OSI IS-IS Intra-domain Routing Protocol
summary: A republication of the ISO 10589 specification for the OSI IS-IS intra-domain routing protocol, as a service to the Internet community. It is not an Internet standard. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 7142.

eli5.summary: Routers learn the whole map and pick the shortest road. This is a copy of another standards group's rule book for that, put here for convenience.

subtitle: A hierarchical link-state protocol for routing inside an administrative domain.

tldr.problem: Routers in a domain need a protocol to discover each other, exchange information about network topology, and calculate the best paths to reach every other router. A single flat routing scheme does not scale well for large domains.
tldr.mechanism: IS-IS routers flood link state advertisements throughout the domain. Each router builds a complete map of the topology, then uses a shortest-path algorithm to compute the best route to each destination. The domain is divided into areas: Level 1 routers route within their area, and Level 2 routers route between areas.
tldr.outcome: Routers converge on consistent routing tables and forward packets along optimal paths. The protocol is robust, efficient, and can handle large, complex networks. It was later superseded by RFC 7142, which represents a consolidation of the standard.

today: RFC 1142 is Historic. It was superseded by RFC 7142, which consolidates the IS-IS specification. RFC 1142 remains a comprehensive reference for understanding the ISO IS-IS protocol, but new implementations should follow RFC 7142 instead.

sections.title: Introduction to IS-IS
sections.content:
RFC 1142 publishes the ISO 10589 specification for the IS-IS intra-domain routing protocol. IS-IS is a protocol for Intermediate Systems (routers) to exchange routing information within a single administrative routing domain. It is designed to work in conjunction with ISO 8473, the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol, and ISO 9542, which handles End System to Intermediate System communication.

The protocol operates at the Network Layer and enables routers to discover each other, learn the topology of the network, and compute shortest paths for forwarding packets. Unlike some earlier routing approaches, IS-IS assumes a connectionless underlying service and supports a wide variety of subnetwork types, including LANs, point-to-point links, X.25 networks, and other technologies.

This standard represents the OSI community's approach to intra-domain routing, published as an RFC to make it available to the Internet community. The specification is comprehensive, covering not only the basic routing algorithm but also procedures for managing the database, handling special topologies, and providing security through authentication.
sections.eli5: IS-IS is a rule book that explains how routers tell each other about the network so everyone can figure out where to send packets. It works for all kinds of networks: wired, wireless, big networks, small ones.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
IS-IS is a link-state routing protocol, which means each router learns the complete topology of its routing domain. Routers use this complete picture to calculate their own routing tables independently, ensuring consistency across the network.

The protocol operates through several key processes. The Update Process creates and propagates Link State PDUs (LSPs), which are messages describing the router's directly connected neighbors and the costs of reaching them. The Decision Process calculates shortest paths using the Dijkstra algorithm (shortest path first, or SPF). The Forwarding Process uses the computed paths to actually route packets. The Receive Process handles incoming PDUs from other routers and from higher protocol layers.

To prevent flooding the network with unnecessary control traffic, LSPs are generated both periodically and when topology changes occur. Each router floods LSPs throughout the domain so that every other router receives a copy, using a mechanism where each router forwards LSPs it receives to all neighbors except the one it came from.
sections.eli5: IS-IS has four main jobs: create maps (update), read maps and plan routes (decision), actually deliver packets (forward), and listen for messages from neighbors (receive). When the network changes, routers quickly tell everyone about it.

sections.title: Two-Level Hierarchical Routing
sections.content:
A key innovation of IS-IS is its support for hierarchical routing, which allows very large domains to scale efficiently. Instead of treating the entire domain as flat, IS-IS divides it into areas, organized in two levels:

Level 1 (Intra-Area Routing): Level 1 routers maintain detailed knowledge of the topology within their own area. When a Level 1 router needs to send a packet to a destination outside its area, it forwards it to the nearest Level 2 router (called an Attached router) within the same area, regardless of the actual destination area. This allows Level 1 routers to ignore the structure of other areas entirely.

Level 2 (Inter-Area Routing): Level 2 routers maintain a complete map of the entire domain, tracking paths to all areas. They route packets between areas and to external destinations. A Level 2 router also acts as a Level 1 router in its own area, so it maintains both Level 1 and Level 2 routing information.

This two-level design allows domains to grow very large. Level 1 routers need only know about their local area, keeping their databases small and their routing computation fast. Level 2 routers carry the burden of inter-area routing. If an area becomes partitioned due to link failures, Level 2 paths can be used to repair the partition, ensuring that disconnected parts can still communicate.
sections.eli5: Think of the postal system: mail carriers (Level 1) know their local neighborhood well and hand off packages destined elsewhere to regional hubs (Level 2). The hubs move mail between regions. This way, each carrier does not have to know about every city on Earth.

sections.title: Addressing and Network Structure
sections.content:
All routers and end systems within a routing domain must have addresses that conform to a specified structure. A system's address is called its Network Entity Title (NET), which consists of three parts: an area address (variable length), a system ID (1 to 8 octets), and an NSAP selector (1 octet).

The area address identifies which area a system belongs to. All systems in the same area must share the same area address. A Level 1 router maintains one or more area addresses; Level 2 routers manage the collection of all area addresses in the domain.

The system ID uniquely identifies a router within its area (Level 1) or within the entire domain (Level 2). All systems in an area must choose the same length for this field. This structured addressing allows routers to make routing decisions based on prefixes: Level 1 routers can determine whether a destination is in their area by checking if the area address matches.

IS-IS also supports pseudonodes, a technique for handling broadcast subnetworks like LANs. On a LAN with multiple routers, one router is elected as a Designated Intermediate System and generates a pseudonode, representing the LAN as a single node in the topology. This simplifies the routing computation and reduces the size of routing advertisements.
sections.eli5: Each router has an address like a postal code (area) plus a street address (system ID). Routers in the same area have the same postal code. On shared networks like Wi-Fi, one router acts as a representative (a pseudonode) so others don't have to track each connection separately.

sections.title: Protocol Data Units and Messages
sections.content:
IS-IS routers exchange several types of control messages:

Link State PDUs (LSPs) are the primary routing information packets. An LSP contains the source router's ID, lists its direct neighbors and the cost to reach each one, and includes information about areas and reachable prefixes. Because a router's adjacency list may be large, IS-IS allows a single logical LSP to be divided into multiple physical PDUs, numbered 0, 1, 2, and so on. Each LSP includes a sequence number, a remaining lifetime counter (for garbage collection), and a checksum to detect corruption.

Hello PDUs (IIHs) are sent periodically on each link to establish and maintain neighbor relationships. They allow routers to discover each other and to detect when a neighbor has failed.

Sequence Number PDUs (SNPs) serve a reliability function. A Complete Sequence Numbers PDU (CSNP) is multicast periodically on broadcast links by the Designated Intermediate System, listing all LSPs in the database. Routers receiving it can check if they have the same LSPs. A Partial Sequence Numbers PDU (PSNP) acknowledges receipt of LSPs on point-to-point links and can request missing ones.

All LSPs are flooded throughout the domain (or area, for Level 1 LSPs) using a controlled flooding mechanism: each router forwards received LSPs to all neighbors except the one it came from, with rate limiting to prevent congestion.
sections.eli5: Routers send three main message types: maps (LSPs) describing the network, hellos saying 'I am here,' and acknowledgments confirming 'I got your map.' Routers make sure everyone gets the latest maps by passing them along, but not so fast that they clog the network.

sections.title: Shortest Path Calculation
sections.content:
Once a router has received and stored LSPs from other routers, the Decision Process calculates the best routes using the Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm, also known as Dijkstra's algorithm. This algorithm computes the minimum-cost path from the local router to each destination, based on a set of routing metrics.

IS-IS supports multiple routing metrics simultaneously, allowing different service classes to use different criteria for path selection. For example, one metric might measure delay, another might measure bandwidth, and another might measure financial cost. A router can support up to four metrics. Each instance of the SPF algorithm runs independently for each metric at each level (Level 1 and Level 2), so a router might execute the algorithm many times.

The algorithm produces a set of legal paths to each destination. A legal path is either a minimum cost path (the lowest metric sum), an equal minimum cost path (tied with other paths of the same lowest cost), or a downstream path (one that makes progress toward the destination but may not be strictly shortest). If multiple paths have equal cost, IS-IS can load split traffic across them.

To ensure consistency, the standard specifies a deterministic algorithm for pruning excess paths based on adjacency type, metric sum, and neighbor ID. This ensures that all routers in the domain converge to the same set of paths and never create routing loops.
sections.eli5: Each router does its homework: it looks at the maps (LSPs) it received and figures out the shortest road to every other router. If there are multiple shortest roads, it can use all of them to spread traffic. The algorithm is carefully designed so all routers agree on the same shortest roads.

sections.title: Router Operations and Database Management
sections.content:
When the network topology changes (a link goes up or down, or a metric changes), the affected router generates a new LSP with an updated sequence number and floods it. Other routers receive the new LSP, update their databases, and if the change affects their own routing tables, they run the SPF algorithm again.

IS-IS uses sequence numbers to determine which copy of an LSP is newest. A sequence number is a 4-octet value that increases from 1 to a maximum. Routers compare sequence numbers to decide whether to accept or reject received LSPs. If a router sees an LSP with a higher sequence number than what it has stored, it accepts the newer version. If two LSPs have the same sequence number but different checksums, the router treats the one with zero remaining lifetime as newest, indicating a purge.

To clean up old information, each LSP has a Remaining Lifetime counter, set to 20 minutes (the MaxAge) when generated. As the LSP propagates, the counter is decremented. When it reaches zero, the LSP expires and is removed from databases. This prevents stale routing information from persisting indefinitely if a router crashes and never advertises an update.

The Link State Database must remain consistent across all routers. To detect and recover from inconsistencies, routers periodically exchange Complete Sequence Numbers PDUs that list all LSPs in the database, allowing each router to identify any missing or old entries and request updates.

If a router runs out of memory to store LSPs, it enters an overload state, setting a bit in its own LSP to tell other routers not to use it as a forwarding path. This prevents packets from being dropped due to corrupted routing information.
sections.eli5: When something changes, the affected router broadcasts a new map with a higher version number. Other routers check if it is newer than what they have, and if so, they update their own maps and recalculate routes. Old maps expire after 20 minutes so stale information does not linger. Routers periodically swap lists of what they have to make sure they are synchronized.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
IS-IS includes a mechanism for routers to authenticate each other using passwords. Each Level 1 area can have a password, and the Level 2 domain as a whole can have a different password. When a router generates an LSP, it may include an authentication field containing the password. Receiving routers check the password; if it does not match a configured value, they discard the LSP and log an authentication failure event.

The standard notes that this password mechanism provides only weak authentication, protecting mainly against accidental misconfiguration errors. It does not protect against a determined attacker who can read network traffic. The design allows for stronger authentication mechanisms to be added in the future without changing the core PDU structure or protocol exchange machinery.

Beyond authentication, IS-IS has several robustness mechanisms. Every LSP is protected by a checksum (using the same checksum function as ISO 8473) to detect memory corruption. Routers periodically verify checksums of all LSPs in memory; if corruption is detected, the router disables itself until the database is cleared and rebuilt. The two-way connectivity check ensures that a link is considered up only if both routers report it, preventing loops due to unidirectional failures.

The protocol also includes mechanisms to prevent deadlock (buffer exhaustion), to handle temporarily corrupted LSPs, and to tolerate imprecise parameter settings.
sections.eli5: Routers can use a password to verify that a map came from a trusted router, not an imposter. It is not perfect security, but it stops honest mistakes. Routers also check that messages did not get corrupted in memory. If something looks broken, the router essentially quarantines itself rather than spreading bad information.

sections.title: Design Goals and Architecture
sections.content:
IS-IS was designed with a comprehensive set of goals that influenced every aspect of the protocol. Some key objectives include:

Scalability: The two-level hierarchy allows the protocol to support domains of essentially unlimited size.

Efficiency: The protocol minimizes both processing load and memory usage. Link state flooding is more efficient than distance-vector flooding for large domains, and the hierarchical structure keeps Level 1 routers' databases small.

Robustness: The protocol recovers from transient errors (lost or corrupted LSPs), tolerates imprecise parameter settings, and handles a wide range of network types.

Simplicity and Performance Tuning: The design is sufficiently simple that operators can tune parameters and isolate failures.

Determinism: Routes depend only on topology, not on history. The same topology always converges to the same set of routes, preventing unpredictable behavior.

Heterogeneity: The protocol works over a mixture of subnetwork types (LANs, point-to-point links, X.25, PSTN) and system types.

Evolution: The protocol allows orderly transition from one version to another without shutting down the entire domain.

Some goals are explicitly not part of the design: the protocol does not guarantee delivery of all packets, does not adapt routes based on traffic load (only topology), and does not support source-destination routing. These are deliberate trade-offs to keep the protocol manageable and efficient.
sections.eli5: The designers wanted IS-IS to handle huge networks, work on any kind of connection, be easy to tune, and converge quickly on the right routes. They also decided some things were not worth doing, like trying to optimize routes based on how busy the network was—that would be too complicated.

sections.title: Scope and Limitations
sections.content:
IS-IS is an intra-domain routing protocol, meaning it is designed to route within a single administrative domain. It does not handle inter-domain routing. A separate protocol is needed to connect multiple domains together; IS-IS can carry reachable address prefixes learned from other domains at the domain boundaries, but it does not itself handle the inter-domain exchange.

The protocol assumes certain guarantees from the underlying subnetwork and data link layers. For example, on point-to-point links, it assumes the link provides ordered, in-sequence delivery of packets. On broadcast links, it assumes a low probability of loss due to corruption or receiver overrun. These assumptions are generally met by modern networks like Ethernet and point-to-point serial links.

IS-IS also assumes that the Internet layer (ISO 8473) is available to deliver packets, and that End System to Intermediate System connectivity is available (ISO 9542) to allow end systems to discover and reach routers. The specification includes detailed procedures for interacting with these components through subnetwork-dependent convergence functions.

The standard is comprehensive, covering not just the basic algorithm but also detailed procedures for system management (setting parameters, monitoring statistics), handling special topologies, managing the database lifecycle, and implementing the protocol efficiently on real systems.
sections.eli5: IS-IS is designed to work inside one company's or organization's network. To connect to other networks, you would use a different tool. IS-IS assumes the wiring and data links are reliable enough that routers can focus on routing, not on fixing corrupted bits.
